project_name: Security and Privacy Requirements Analysis Tool
initial_requirements: Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.

topics.topic_content: Shared terminology for requirements, goals, and policies

slots.key: Definitions of goal, scenario, policy, and requirement
slots.value: A goal is the business or system objective, such as protecting customer data or making a service usable under certain constraints. A policy is the rule or obligation to follow, usually from law, corporate standards, or security guidance. A requirement is the specific statement written so the system can meet that goal and comply with that policy.

revisions.new_value: A goal is the business or system objective, such as protecting customer data or making a service usable under certain constraints. A policy is the rule or obligation to follow, usually from law, corporate standards, or security guidance. A requirement is the specific statement written so the system can meet that goal and comply with that policy.

slots.value: The workbench should show which requirement supports which goal, and which policy or legal source justified that goal or requirement. It should represent many-to-many relationships cleanly, including cases where one requirement maps to several goals and one policy drives many requirements. It should also show overlaps, dependencies, reused policy interpretations, and derivation links when a requirement comes from another requirement or a scenario, so reviewers can see the reasoning behind the final statement. Derived-from links should stay visible even if the source item is later revised or marked inactive. They should be able to chain through multiple levels when that history matters, but the UI should still make the direct parent clear so the trail isn’t ambiguous. Derived links should be treated differently from direct goal or policy traces, since direct trace is more about justification or compliance while derived-from is more about lineage.

slots.key: Validation rules for trace links and classification consistency
slots.value: Require trace links when a requirement claims to come from a policy, and flag missing or inconsistent classifications rather than silently accepting them. Fast-path handling is acceptable only for routine, low-risk actions based on an approved template or previously validated pattern, and only if the system still captures who did it, what changed, when it happened, and which source policy or requirement it came from; do not allow skipping extra steps when the action affects sensitive classifications, legal compliance, access permissions, or introduces a new trace link. Before approving a locked classification change, check whether the proposed change would break existing traceability, alter who can see or edit the artifact, invalidate compliance evidence already attached, or leave dependent goals, requirements, or policies inconsistent. Approve only when downstream effects are understood and recorded; otherwise keep the classification locked.

topics.topic_content: Rules governing analysis content and traceability

slots.value: Analysts must record where each requirement came from, what part of the rule it satisfies, and any assumptions or exceptions; traceability must be strong enough for review, audit, and comparison across analysts. The interviewee also stated that a requirement should be justified by a goal and anchored to a real policy source. The workbench should show which requirement supports which goal, and which policy or legal source justified that goal or requirement. It must represent many-to-many relationships cleanly, including cases where one requirement maps to several goals and one policy drives many requirements. Overlaps and dependencies should be captured, and if a requirement was derived through another requirement or a scenario, that connection should be visible for reasoning. The tool should require trace links where a requirement claims to come from a policy. It should capture the specific source policy reference, the exact part of the policy that justifies the goal, a short rationale explaining the connection, and who made the trace and when. The trace may be supported by several policies together or be indirect through a requirement or scenario, as long as the relationship is explainable. Overlapping traces should be visible rather than hidden under a single path, and if an item belongs to multiple paths, the tool should show all relevant links and make clear which link is primary when the team has designated one. Nothing should be lost just because it appears in more than one analysis route, and shared dependencies should be easy for reviewers to understand without confusion. The derived-from link should stay visible even if the source item is later revised or marked inactive, because people still need to understand where the requirement came from. It should be able to chain through multiple levels when that history matters, but the UI should still make the direct parent clear so the trail isn’t ambiguous. Derived links should be treated differently from direct goal or policy traces, since they mean lineage rather than justification/compliance. The trace should preserve intermediate goals or policy versions when that helps explain the justification path, while keeping the direct policy link prominent for quick access to the authoritative source. During initial rollout, migrate active projects, authoritative source documents, and anything needed to maintain traceability for current work first; older drafts, duplicates, and reference material not being used right now can stay in the old tools for a while, especially if moving them would create confusion. Sensitive or messy material that needs cleanup before import should be held back until validated, and the main rule is to bring in what people need to work on immediately, not every historical artifact on day one. Users may take the fast path for routine, low-risk actions based on an approved template or previously validated pattern, as long as the system still captures who did it, what changed, when it happened, and which source policy or requirement it came from. Fast path skipping is not allowed when the action affects sensitive classifications, legal compliance, access permissions, or introduces a new trace link.

slots.value: New analysts should be able to get started with basic capture and trace tasks with minimal guidance, such as entering goals, scenarios, and linking a requirement to its source. slots.key: Role-based access control and sensitive material handling
slots.value: Different roles must see and do different things, with access control shaped by organizational context; for sensitive projects, tighter access controls apply, especially for guests and analysts not assigned to the project. New analysts may draft entries, but cannot finalize or publish traces without review by a project manager or more experienced analyst. Access may be limited to approved devices or trusted networks, driven by project sensitivity and administrator policy, with extra approval only for the most restricted material. In low-risk projects, simple editing, reclassifying, and linking to ordinary source types should be open once new analysts have learned the workflow, but final approval or anything that changes official compliance wording stays behind a more senior role. Especially sensitive source types, such as legal interpretations or policy exceptions, may still require a review step even in low-risk projects. Project managers should be able to review, comment, compare analyses, and check traceability, but they shouldn’t have unrestricted editing unless that’s part of their role on the project. slots.value: Analysts must record which requirement supports which goal, and which policy or legal source justified that goal or requirement; the workbench should also represent overlaps, dependencies, and derived connections so reviewers can see the reasoning, not just the final statement. It should capture the specific source policy reference, the exact part of the policy that justifies the goal, a short rationale explaining the connection, and who made the trace and when, so reviewers can see whether it was added deliberately and by whom. The tool should allow traces supported by several policies together or indirect links through a requirement or scenario, as long as the relationship is still explainable. Overlapping traces should be visible rather than hidden under a single path, with all relevant links shown when an item belongs to multiple paths and any designated primary link made clear. When a requirement traces back to a source policy, the trace should preserve intermediate goals or policy versions when that helps explain the justification path, while keeping the direct policy link prominent so people can quickly get to the authoritative source.
